## What You Will Learn {.content-slide}

By the end, you should be able to explain:

1. How to read the support-ticket workflow diagram
2. What an AI skill is, and how it differs from a deterministic automation
3. How to turn process steps into skills
4. Why skills need clear inputs and outputs
5. What an orchestrator does
6. **Where human-in-the-loop pauses belong, and how they look in code**
7. **How the same skills and data can be invoked via MCP — and what changes when "the data moves" from a local file to a shared remote source**
8. How the browser demo lets you inspect the workflow
9. How a one-off fix becomes a reusable FAQ entry

::: notes
Frame this as workflow design, not programming. The technical details exist to
make the business process visible and testable.
:::

## The Process We Are Automating {.content-slide}

![](assets/customer-ticket-process-genai-page-2.png){fig-alt="Swimlane diagram for customer support ticket resolution" .width-full}

::: notes
This is the anchor diagram for the whole deck. It has three lanes: User, GenAI
Assistant, and IT specialist. The repo turns this picture into a working demo.
:::

## How to Read the Diagram {.content-slide}

The diagram shows:

- **lanes**: Who owns each action
- **boxes**: Work to be done
- **diamonds**: Decisions or branch points
- **arrows**: Handoffs from one step to the next
- **loops**: What happens when the first answer is rejected

Which steps can AI handle, which steps need human review, and how do we keep the handoffs visible?

::: notes
Students should first read this as a business process map. Do not start with
code. Start with roles, work, decisions, and handoffs.
:::

## The Three Lanes {.content-slide}

**User**

Submits the ticket and later accepts or rejects the answer.

**GenAI Assistant**

Receives, classifies, checks FAQ, drafts, sends, and closes routine work.

**IT Specialist**

Handles cases where the issue needs expert diagnosis or approval.

::: notes
The workflow is not "AI does everything." It is an AI-assisted process with
clear escalation paths.
:::

## Start with Skills {.section-slide}

## Skill vs. Automation {.content-slide}

These are **not** the same thing. The distinction is the most important
slide in this deck.

**Skill** (Anthropic definition)

A folder with `SKILL.md` that an LLM agent loads to decide *when* to
invoke it. **LLM judgement happens on every run** — either the agent
itself supplies it, or the script inside calls an LLM directly.

**Automation**

A deterministic script that runs without an LLM. Rule-based code,
table lookups, templates. The orchestrator runs it and no agent is needed.

::: notes
Both produce the same kind of JSON envelope so the orchestrator can drive
them identically. The difference is purely about where AI judgement lives.
:::

## A Skill Has Two Runtime Modes {.content-slide}

The same skill folder runs in two settings:

| Runtime | Who provides the LLM? | What the script does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside an agent (Claude Code, Codex) | The agent itself | Could be deterministic — agent reads `SKILL.md`, supplies the judgement, the script just records the result |
| Terminal / orchestrator / CI | (no agent in the loop) | **Script must call the LLM itself** (e.g. via `utils.connect.ask_json()`) |

This repo's two skills take the second approach in both modes — they
always call the LLM themselves. That means the **same code path** runs
from terminal, the web demo, the test suite (mocked), and from an LLM
agent. One set of code, one set of tests.

::: notes
The classroom takeaway: a skill is "an agent-invocable procedure", not
"a script that always contains an LLM call." Two valid design choices
for where the LLM judgement happens. We picked the path that keeps the
demo testable offline.
:::

## Where Does AI Live? {.content-slide}

This repo has twelve workflow steps. **Only three are skills:**

`skills/check-faq-resolution/`

An LLM decides whether the FAQ knowledge base resolves the ticket.

`skills/investigate-specialist-solution/`

An LLM acts as the assigned specialist and produces a diagnosis plus
customer-safe action.

`skills/draft-faq-candidate/`

After a specialist's solution is accepted by the customer, an LLM
drafts a candidate FAQ entry so the next similar ticket can match it.
A supervisor approves or skips before it lands in the knowledge base.

## Where Does AI NOT Live? {.content-slide}

The other nine steps live under `automations/` — receive, classify,
escalate, draft FAQ response, draft specialist response,
**review-specialist-draft** (HITL gate), send, verify feedback,
**approve-faq-promotion** (HITL gate), audit. All deterministic.

That is on purpose:

- AI earns its keep on **genuine judgement** — the FAQ-or-not call, the
  specialist diagnosis, the FAQ-candidate draft. Each is easy to verify
  when wrong.
- Deterministic steps are easily testable and give an auditable rationale
  instead of "the model said so."
- HITL gates are also deterministic Python — they record a human
  decision and patch the next step's input. The supervisor is the
  judgement, not the script.
- "AI-assisted workflow" ≠ "Every step is an LLM call."

::: notes
The two HITL automations (review-specialist-draft, approve-faq-promotion)
are deliberately not skills: there's no LLM judgement inside the script;
the human is the judgement. The orchestrator simply pauses on those
steps until the supervisor submits a decision through the web UI.
:::

## Why Two Folders, Not One? {.content-slide}

```text
skills/                         # only LLM-based steps
├── check-faq-resolution/
│   ├── SKILL.md                  # agent contract
│   ├── README.md
│   └── scripts/
├── investigate-specialist-solution/
│   ├── SKILL.md
│   ├── README.md
│   └── scripts/
└── draft-faq-candidate/
    ├── SKILL.md
    ├── README.md
    └── scripts/

automations/                    # deterministic steps
├── receive-ticket/                 # no SKILL.md, no LLM
├── classify-prioritize-ticket/
├── draft-faq-response/
├── escalate-to-specialist/
├── draft-specialist-response/
├── review-specialist-draft/        # HITL pause
├── send-customer-response/
├── verify-feedback-close-or-reopen/
├── approve-faq-promotion/          # HITL pause
└── audit-ticket-process/

mcp_servers/            # optional: two MCP servers (skills + data)
install.sh              # one root script registers all skills
```

The folder is the signal: if it has `SKILL.md`, an LLM agent can load it.
If it doesn't, the step is plain Python and nothing more.

::: notes
The split makes the AI surface area legible to a non-technical reviewer.
You can answer "where is AI used?" by listing the folders under `skills/`.
A single `bash install.sh` at the repo root symlinks every skill into
`.claude/skills/` — auto-discovered from `skills/*/SKILL.md`. The
`mcp_servers/` folder is a separate teaching example covered later.
:::

## Why Not One Big AI Prompt? {.content-slide}

One giant prompt would be hard to manage.

Small skills are better because they are:

- easier to understand
- easier to improve
- easier to test
- easier to audit
- easier to assign to a process owner
- easier to escalate when something goes wrong

::: notes
This is a core management lesson: modularity is governance. It makes process
quality observable.
:::

## Skill Design Canvas {.content-slide}

For each skill, define six things:

- **Trigger:** a new ticket exists
- **Input data:** ticket text, customer tier, affected system
- **Work:** classify and prioritize
- **Output data:** category, priority, rationale
- **Next action:** check FAQ
- **Human review trigger:** low confidence or missing information

::: notes
Students can reuse this canvas for any workflow: admissions, claims, HR,
procurement, loan approval, etc.
:::

## From Diagram Step to Code {.content-slide}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Automations** (deterministic)

- Receive ticket → `automations/receive-ticket`
- Classify + priority → `automations/classify-prioritize-ticket`
- Draft FAQ reply → `automations/draft-faq-response`
- Escalate → `automations/escalate-to-specialist`
- Draft specialist reply → `automations/draft-specialist-response`
- **Review draft (HITL)** → `automations/review-specialist-draft`
- Send → `automations/send-customer-response`
- Verify feedback → `automations/verify-feedback-close-or-reopen`
- **Approve FAQ promotion (HITL)** → `automations/approve-faq-promotion`
- Audit → `automations/audit-ticket-process`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Skills** (LLM-based)

- FAQ resolution? → `skills/check-faq-resolution`
- Specialist diagnosis → `skills/investigate-specialist-solution`
- FAQ candidate draft → `skills/draft-faq-candidate`
:::
::::::

::: notes
Twelve steps total: nine deterministic automations (two of which are HITL
pause points) plus three LLM-based skills. The HITL automations
demonstrate that "pause for a human" is just another deterministic step
with the same envelope contract.
:::

## Example Automation: Classify and Prioritize {.content-slide}

A deterministic step. **No LLM call.**

Input:

- ticket subject and description
- affected system
- customer tier
- urgency
- reference categories and priority rules

Output:

- assigned category (keyword + system-match score)
- assigned priority (additive rule)
- recommended specialist group
- rationale and confidence
- next action: `check-faq-resolution`

::: notes
The category score is keyword overlap plus a system-typicality bonus. The
priority is `tier + urgency + category_bump`. Both fit on a page and are
auditable line-by-line — exactly why AI is not needed here.
:::

## Example Skill: Check FAQ (LLM) {.content-slide}

Input to the LLM:

- ticket details
- triage category
- the active FAQ knowledge base

Decision the LLM must return as JSON:

```text
Strong FAQ match?
  Yes -> draft FAQ response
  No  -> escalate to specialist
```

Output:

- `faq_match_found`
- `faq_id`
- `match_confidence`
- `required_customer_info_available`
- `recommended_next_step`

::: notes
The most important branch point in the workflow — and the first place an
LLM earns its keep. The judgement is "does this FAQ actually resolve this
ticket?" — a comparison that's easy to verify when wrong.
:::

## Example Skill: Investigate Specialist Solution (LLM) {.content-slide}

When the FAQ branch can't resolve the ticket, the workflow asks an LLM to
**act as the assigned specialist** and propose a fix.

Input to the LLM:

- ticket (subject, description, affected system, urgency, steps tried)
- triage (category, priority, specialist group)
- escalation handoff and the specific question
- specialist profile (group, seniority)

JSON the LLM must return:

- `root_cause`
- `diagnostic_steps`
- `evidence_reviewed`
- `solution_summary` (customer-safe)
- `customer_action_required`
- `confidence`
- `requires_follow_up_flag`

If the escalation flagged missing customer info, confidence is **capped at
0.60** during normalisation — that ticket always lands in human review.

::: notes
This is the second LLM step. It is structurally identical to FAQ check: a
JSON-only prompt, a validated response, deterministic post-processing.
Same pattern, different prompt.
:::

## Example Automation: Verify Feedback {.content-slide}

After the response is sent, the customer replies. **Rule-based, no LLM.**

The feedback automation decides:

- accepted (positive phrases)
  - **FAQ branch** → audit & close
  - **Specialist branch** → route to `draft-faq-candidate` (institutional
    learning: turn the one-off fix into a reusable FAQ entry)
- rejected (negative phrases), first time → reopen and escalate
- ambiguous → ask for clarification
- rejected twice → close unresolved (loop-prevention guard)

::: notes
This is where loops enter the process. Loops need explicit rules or they
can run forever. The "accepted on specialist branch → FAQ candidate"
routing is the bridge between solving one ticket and improving the
knowledge base — a key institutional-learning loop.
:::

## Human-in-the-Loop Gates {.section-slide}

## Two Pause Points on the Specialist Branch {.content-slide}

The workflow inserts **two human-review pauses** on the specialist
branch. Both are deterministic automations, not skills — there is no
LLM judgment inside the script. The orchestrator simply stops on those
steps and waits for the supervisor's decision from the web UI.

| Gate | When | Supervisor action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `review-specialist-draft` | After `draft-specialist-response`, before `send-customer-response` | Edit + Approve, or Reject (re-investigate, bounded to one retry) |
| `approve-faq-promotion` | After the customer accepts the specialist solution | Edit + Approve & Add to FAQ, or Skip |

The FAQ branch has neither gate. Its answer comes from a curated FAQ
entry that's already been reviewed — no second review needed.

::: notes
Why only the specialist branch: novel solutions need supervision; reuse
of an existing FAQ entry doesn't. Mirrors how a real IT team would handle
both flows.
:::

## Pause 1: Review the Specialist Draft {.content-slide}

The LLM drafted the customer-facing reply. Before it's sent, a
supervisor can:

- **Approve & Send** — optionally edit the text (the original LLM draft
  is preserved in `draft_text` for audit; the edited copy goes into
  `sent_text`).
- **Reject** — orchestrator re-runs `investigate-specialist-solution`
  with the reviewer's notes, redrafts, and pauses again. A second reject
  is forced through as an approve so the loop is bounded.

Decision is recorded in `data/working/specialist_draft_reviews.csv`
with the original text, edited text, decision, retry count, and
reviewer notes.

::: notes
Bounded retry is the loop-prevention guard. The supervisor can always
edit-and-approve to ship a custom answer; reject is the "send it back"
button, used at most once per ticket.
:::

One new node, one bounded back-edge. Cost: one supervisor click per

:::

## Pause 2: Approve the FAQ Promotion {.content-slide}

Triggered only when a specialist solution was accepted by the customer.
A new LLM skill, `draft-faq-candidate`, pre-fills a candidate FAQ entry
from the ticket + specialist solution: category, system, issue pattern,
symptoms, solution steps, required customer info.

The supervisor sees the pre-filled form and either:

- **Approve & Add to FAQ** — optionally edit any field. The orchestrator
  appends a row to the per-run `data/raw/faq_knowledge_base.csv` with
  `owner=workflow_promotion`. Future tickets in the same run can match
  against it.
- **Skip** — the decision is logged but the FAQ KB is untouched.

This is the institutional-learning loop: one supervised approval turns
a one-off specialist fix into a reusable knowledge-base entry.

::: notes
Pedagogy: the LLM does the tedious pre-fill work; the human does the
"should we publish this?" judgment. Same pattern as a real KB-curation
workflow.
:::

## A Skill Must Leave Evidence {.content-slide}

Each skill should leave behind:

- what it read
- what it decided
- why it decided that
- what file or artifact it wrote
- what should happen next

In the demo, this appears in the **Skill input / output** panel.

::: notes
This is the bridge from AI output to auditability. Students should look for
evidence, not just final answers.
:::

## Step Packages: Two Shapes {.content-slide}

A **skill** folder has the agent contract:

```text
skills/check-faq-resolution/
  SKILL.md                       # when to invoke (agent reads this)
  README.md
  scripts/check_faq_resolution.py   # calls an LLM
```

All skills are registered with one `bash install.sh` at the repo root.

An **automation** folder is simpler — no agent contract:

```text
automations/receive-ticket/
  README.md
  scripts/receive_ticket.py          # deterministic
```

::: notes
The presence of `SKILL.md` is the signal: if you see it, an LLM agent can
load this step. If you don't, the step is plain Python.
:::

## The Step Contract {.content-slide}

Every step script — skill or automation — takes the same flags so the
orchestrator can drive any of them:

- `--ticket-id`
- `--data-dir` / `--out-dir`
- `--workflow-run-id` / `--step-id`
- `--mode {live,demo}` — live = use only fresh working data;
  demo = also accept seeded historical rows
- `--idempotency-mode {skip,replace}` — re-running the same step is safe
- `--json` — emit the envelope instead of a text summary

The shared parser lives in `lib/ticketing_common.py`. New steps inherit
the contract; they do not redesign it.

::: notes
This is the boring-on-purpose part. Uniform flags = uniform orchestration.
The orchestrator does not need to know what any given step does — only how
to invoke it.
:::

## The Envelope: Every Step Talks Like This {.content-slide}

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "skill_name": "check-faq-resolution",
  "ticket_id": "TKT-00042",
  "next_action": "draft-faq-response",
  "confidence": 0.91,
  "review_required": false,
  "artifact_refs": ["working/faq_decisions.csv"],
  "outputs": {…},
  "error": null
}
```

- `next_action` → routes the orchestrator.
- `review_required` → routes a human.
- `artifact_refs` → audit trail.

(The field is `skill_name` for historical reasons — it carries the step
name whether the step is a skill or an automation.)

::: notes
Process governance ≈ the envelope. Anything you want oversight on goes here.
:::

## Then Add Orchestration {.section-slide}

## What Is the Orchestrator? {.content-slide}

The orchestrator is the workflow manager. It does not classify, draft, or solve tickets. It does:

- Remember which skill is next
- Run one skill at a time
- Pass the right ticket and run IDs
- Read the skill's `next_action`
- Pause when customer or human input is needed
- Update the web page

::: notes
This is the answer to the earlier confusion: the orchestrator is not a domain
skill. It is the control layer that coordinates the skills.
:::

## Why the Orchestrator Is Code {.content-slide}

The orchestrator is code because control flow must be predictable.

It should be:

- BORING
- Explicit
- Testable
- Repeatable
- Easy to debug

The skills can contain business logic. The orchestrator should not improvise
the route.

::: notes
Analogy: the orchestrator is like a workflow engine, conductor, or air traffic
controller. The skills are the specialized work teams.
:::

## The Mental Model {.content-slide}

* Orchestrator: workflow engine
* Skill: Focused work unit
* Working CSVs: Shared case file
* JSON envelope: Handoff note
* Web page: Control room dashboard

::: notes
Use this vocabulary consistently. It helps students distinguish process design, execution, data, and user interface.
:::

## How Skills Talk to the Orchestrator {.content-slide}

Each skill returns a structured handoff:

```json
{
  "skill_name": "check-faq-resolution",
  "status": "ok",
  "ticket_id": "WEB-1234ABCD",
  "next_action": "draft-faq-response"
}
```

The orchestrator reads `next_action` and stores the next skill.

::: notes
This is the simplest possible control contract. The skill says what happened
and what should happen next.
:::

## Orchestration Loop {.content-slide}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
%%| fig-height: 3.2
%%{init: {'theme':'default', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize':'6px'}, 'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 12, 'rankSpacing': 10}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A[Current state] --> B[Run next skill]
  B --> C[Skill writes output]
  C --> D[Skill returns next_action]
  D --> E[Orchestrator updates state]
  E --> F{Need human or customer input?}
  F -->|No| A
  F -->|Yes| G[Pause workflow]
```

::: notes
The font + spacing tuning in the %%{init}%% block keeps the diagram
inside the slide without scaling tricks. Same recipe works for any
mermaid block that wants more breathing room.
:::

## Where the Orchestrator Lives {.content-slide}

In this repo:

```text
scripts/orchestrator.py
```

Key object:

```text
TicketWorkflowOrchestrator
```

What to ask Claude/Codex:

```text
Open scripts/orchestrator.py and explain TicketWorkflowOrchestrator
to me using the workflow diagram.
```

::: notes
Students do not need to read the whole file. They need to know where the
control layer is and what to ask an assistant to explain.
:::

## Demo Scenario 1: FAQ Resolution {.content-slide}

Example ticket:

```text
FAQ: customer portal SSO loop
```

Expected path:

```text
receive -> classify/prioritize -> check FAQ
-> draft FAQ response -> send response -> verify feedback -> close
```

Business lesson:

> Good automation handles repeatable work quickly and consistently.

::: notes
Use this as the first demo because it is clean and easy to understand.
:::

## Demo Scenario 2: Human Expert Review {.content-slide}

Example ticket:

```text
Human expert: billing API 502
```

Expected path (HITL gates are **bold**):

```text
receive -> classify/prioritize -> check FAQ
-> escalate -> specialist investigates -> draft specialist response
-> **review-specialist-draft (supervisor approves)**
-> send response -> verify feedback (customer accepts)
-> draft-faq-candidate -> **approve-faq-promotion (supervisor approves)**
-> audit / close
```

Business lesson:

> AI can route and summarize expert work, but some answers still need
> human approval — and a good supervised solution becomes the next
> FAQ entry, not a one-off fix.

::: notes
The supervisor sees two pause panels in this scenario: the draft review
(Approve & Send / Reject) and the FAQ promotion (Approve & Add to FAQ /
Skip). Both write decision rows to `data/working/` for audit.
:::

## Demo Scenario 3: Rejected Answer {.content-slide}

Example ticket:

```text
Reopen: FAQ rejected, then specialist
```

Expected path:

```text
FAQ response sent
-> customer rejects
-> reopen and escalate
-> specialist answer
-> customer accepts
```

Business lesson:

> Feedback loops need rules, ownership, and a stopping condition.

::: notes
This scenario makes the loop on the right side of the diagram concrete.
:::

## Demo Scenario 4: Ambiguous Feedback {.content-slide}

Example ticket:

```text
Feedback: ambiguous customer reply
```

Expected outcome:

```text
request_clarification
```

Business lesson:

> When the signal is unclear, the right workflow action may be to pause.

::: notes
This is a governance point. Not every uncertain input should be forced into an
automated decision.
:::

## Demo Scenario 5: FAQ Promotion in Action {.content-slide}

Pick any specialist-branch scenario (e.g. `Human expert: billing API 502`),
walk through to the customer-accept reply, then watch the
**Supervisor review — promote to FAQ?** panel appear with the LLM's
pre-filled candidate.

Try both choices:

- **Approve & Add to FAQ** — the new entry lands in the per-run
  `data/raw/faq_knowledge_base.csv` with `owner=workflow_promotion`.
  The original `data/raw/` in the repo is **untouched** because the
  orchestrator copies baseline data into `/tmp` per run.
- **Skip** — the decision is logged in
  `data/working/faq_promotion_decisions.csv` and the KB is unchanged.

Business lesson:

> Institutional learning is a workflow concern, not an after-the-fact
> chore. The right time to capture a fix as reusable knowledge is right
> after it's confirmed to work.

::: notes
The per-run /tmp isolation is the key teaching point: students can
freely approve FAQ promotions without polluting the shared dataset.
Each run starts with the original FAQ KB and accumulates its own
additions.
:::

## Run the Scenario Suite {.content-slide}

The repo includes 20 curated examples.

Run them all:

```bash
uv run python automations/summarize-workflow-suite/scripts/summarize_workflow_suite.py
```

Open the HTML report:

```text
/tmp/customer-ticket-process-suite-report.html
```

::: notes
Explain this as quality control. A workflow should be tested against many
scenarios, not just one successful demo.
:::

## A Second Front Door: MCP {.section-slide}

## What Is MCP? {.content-slide}

**Model Context Protocol** — a JSON-RPC protocol an LLM client (Claude
Desktop, Claude Code, Codex) speaks to a long-running server. The
server exposes three things:

- **Tools** — function calls the client can invoke
- **Resources** — read-only context the client can pull in
- **Prompts** — reusable prompt templates surfaced as menu items

MCP earns its keep when ≥2 clients need the same capability and you
don't want to glue paths and credentials into each one.

::: notes
Same idea as a small internal API, but with auto-discovery and a
standard handshake so any compliant LLM client can use it without
custom wiring per client.
:::

## What the Exhibit Exposes {.content-slide}

`mcp_servers/` is an **optional teaching exhibit** — not part of the
orchestrator. It is split deliberately into **two MCP servers** so the
concerns stay separate:

**Skills server** (`mcp_servers.skills_server`) — does work

- `check_faq_resolution(ticket_id)` — wraps `skills/check-faq-resolution`
- `investigate_specialist_solution(ticket_id)` — wraps `skills/investigate-specialist-solution`

**Data server** (`mcp_servers.data_server`) — serves data via URIs

- `tickets://raw`, `tickets://{ticket_id}`
- `faq://kb`  *(local CSV by default; Postgres when `FAQ_KB_URI` is set)*
- `dictionaries://{name}`, `working://{filename}`

The orchestrator stays the canonical path. MCP is a second front door —
same skill scripts, same data files, exposed under a different protocol.

::: notes
Both servers are tiny — each is a FastMCP instance with a few handlers.
The split is for clarity: a server that **does work** is a different
thing from a server that **provides data**. Students can run one or both.
:::

## Wiring Both Servers to a Client {.content-slide}

`.mcp.json` at the repo root (Claude Code reads this automatically;
Claude Desktop takes the same shape under `mcpServers`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "customer-ticket-data": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["run", "python", "-m", "mcp_servers.data_server"]
    },
    "customer-ticket-skills": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["run", "python", "-m", "mcp_servers.skills_server"]
    }
  }
}
```

Run `/mcp` inside Claude Code to verify. Run only one entry if you only
need one server.

::: notes
This is the management argument for MCP: every new consumer of your
skills (or your data) doesn't need a custom integration. They speak one
protocol; each server is the single place that knows where its piece
lives.
:::

## One Env Var Flips Data Local→Remote {.content-slide}

```python
def _load_faq_kb(data_dir: Path) -> pl.DataFrame:
    uri = os.environ.get("FAQ_KB_URI", "").strip()
    if uri:
        return pl.read_database_uri(
            "SELECT * FROM faq_knowledge_base", uri
        )
    return read_csv(data_dir, "raw/faq_knowledge_base.csv")
```

Same helper lives in two places (the data server's `faq://kb` resource
and `skills/check-faq-resolution`). Set `FAQ_KB_URI` to a Postgres
URI and the FAQ knowledge base comes from a shared database;
unset it and the local CSV wins.

::: notes
Six lines of new code, one env var. The teaching point: the *shape* of
the data path is identical — caller still gets a polars DataFrame. The
*source* moved. Show students this side-by-side; it's the smallest
demonstration of the local→remote pattern they'll see.
:::

## MCP Pros and Cons — A Matrix {.content-slide}

Two axes worth separating: **what** is served (skills vs data) and
**where** it lives (local vs remote / shared).

|                   | **Skills (LLM judgement)** | **Data (CSVs, tables)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Local server**  | Each user has their own prompt + LLM key; rapid iteration; nothing to deploy | Each user has their own copy of the data; drift between students is possible |
| **Remote server** | One canonical prompt for everyone; central rate-limit + audit; need auth + uptime | One source of truth; updates propagate; need DB/HTTP infra + credentials |

Trade in plain English:

- **Local + local** — fastest to iterate, hardest to keep consistent.
- **Remote + remote** — most consistent, most operational overhead.
- **Local skills + remote data** *(this repo's example)* — students can
  hack on prompts freely, but everyone sees the same FAQ table the
  instant the instructor updates it.

::: notes
The repo intentionally demonstrates the mixed case. Skills stay local
so students can change prompts and rerun without coordinating with
anyone. Only the FAQ knowledge base — the piece you actually want
*shared* — moves to Postgres. That's the practical pattern: move the
piece that needs to be authoritative, leave the piece you want to
experiment with alone.
:::

## Pros & Cons — Across Clients {.content-slide}

"Across clients" means: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, a scheduled agent,
and a custom Python client — all on the same machine, all wanting the
same capability.

**With local stdio MCP servers** (this repo's default)

- Each client launches its own subprocess; no port, no auth.
- Pro: zero setup; the protocol is the contract.
- Con: each client gets its own process, its own temp `out-dir`, its
  own LLM cache — no shared state.

**With remote HTTP MCP servers**

- All clients talk to one running process.
- Pro: one prompt revision, one rate-limit budget, one audit log.
- Con: needs HTTP transport, auth, and someone running the box.

The repo ships the local stdio version because it's the simplest to
teach. Switching to HTTP is one FastMCP flag plus a deployment story.

::: notes
The orchestrator and the MCP servers both run as plain Python
subprocesses today — the simplest pattern that lets students see what
"different clients, one capability" means. The leap from this to a
shared HTTP MCP server is small.
:::

## Pros & Cons — Across Users {.content-slide}

"Across users" means the whole class, not just one student's laptop.

**Local everything** (one student, one laptop)

- Pro: nothing to deploy, no credentials to manage, fast iteration.
- Con: every student has their own copy of the FAQ KB. The instructor
  pushing a new FAQ row reaches no one until each student regenerates
  data.

**Remote data, local skills + clients** *(this repo's example pattern)*

- Pro: instructor updates one row in Postgres — every student sees it
  on their next ticket. Students still own their prompts and their LLM
  keys.
- Con: needs a database the class can reach (and credentials).
- Trade: small DB hosting cost in exchange for "the FAQ KB is real,
  shared, and changes during the term."

**Remote everything**

- Pro: one canonical workflow, one auditable system, one upgrade.
- Con: a single bug locks the whole class out. Students lose the
  ability to experiment with prompts without permission. Cost and
  latency add up.

::: notes
The classroom pattern that usually works best: move the *facts* (data)
to a shared remote source, leave the *judgement* (prompts, LLM calls)
local. That's exactly what `FAQ_KB_URI` switches on in this repo.
:::

## When MCP Is (and Isn't) Worth It {.content-slide}

**Worth it when:**

- ≥2 LLM clients need the same capability (Desktop + Codex + a
  scheduled job) — MCP saves you N custom integrations.
- A third party needs to invoke your skills without custom glue.
- "Where the data lives" should be a server's problem, not threaded
  through every caller's CLI.

**Not worth it when:**

- One consumer, one process, runs locally — the orchestrator's case.
  Putting MCP in front would just add a process.
- The workflow has its own deterministic control flow that an LLM
  agent shouldn't be encouraged to second-guess.

::: notes
That's why this repo's orchestrator is NOT an MCP server. The exhibit
exposes the two judgement-heavy skills as MCP tools and the data files
as MCP resources, so the same skills and data are callable from any
client; the orchestrator stays a plain CLI demo.
:::

## Build Your Own Workflow {.section-slide}

## Step 1: Draw the Process {.content-slide}

Start the way this deck started:

- who are the lanes?
- what work happens in each lane?
- where are the decisions?
- where are the handoffs?
- where can work loop back?
- where must a human review?

::: notes
Students should not start by coding. They should start with the workflow map.
:::

## Step 2: Identify Candidate Skills {.content-slide}

Look for process boxes that:

- have a clear trigger
- use identifiable data
- produce a useful handoff
- can be evaluated
- are repeated often enough to matter

Avoid skills that are too broad, such as:

```text
Resolve the whole ticket
```

::: notes
This is a practical heuristic for skill design.
:::

## Step 3: Define Skill Contracts {.content-slide}

For each skill, write:

```text
Skill name:
Input data:
Output data:
Decision rules:
Next action:
Human review trigger:
Artifact written:
```

This is the minimum contract for a useful AI workflow step.

::: notes
This mirrors what the repo implements with working CSVs and JSON envelopes.
:::

## Step 4: Define Branches and Stops {.content-slide}

Every workflow needs rules for:

- success path
- exception path
- escalation path
- customer or human feedback
- ambiguous input
- repeated failure
- final close

::: notes
This is where management policy enters the system. A technical team should not
invent these policies alone.
:::

## Step 5: Create Test Scenarios {.content-slide}

Do not test only the happy path.

Create examples for:

- common routine case
- high-priority case
- no-match case
- expert-review case
- rejected answer
- ambiguous answer
- repeated failure

In this repo, examples live in:

```text
data/examples/ticket_scenarios.py
```

::: notes
This reinforces the idea of an operational test portfolio.
:::

## Step 6: Add a Demo Interface {.content-slide}

A good workflow demo should show:

- current state
- completed steps
- branch decisions
- data into and out of each skill
- final output
- where human judgment is required

::: notes
The web app is not just decoration. It is a teaching and debugging interface.
:::

## What to Ask Claude or Codex {.content-slide}

Useful prompts:

```text
Explain this repo using slides/ticket-workflow-orchestration.qmd.
```

```text
Walk me through the Human expert: billing API 502 scenario.
For each step, name the skill, input, output, next action, and any
HITL pause point.
```

```text
Help me design a similar workflow for [loan approval / HR onboarding / claims].
Use the skill design canvas from the deck and decide which steps need
HITL gates.
```

```text
Open mcp_servers/skills_server.py and mcp_servers/data_server.py and
explain what each one exposes, what FAQ_KB_URI switches on, and why
the orchestrator itself is not an MCP server.
```

::: notes
This makes the deck usable as an LLM reference artifact.
:::

## Final Takeaway {.content-slide}

The demo is not just "AI answers support tickets."

It shows how to design an AI workflow:

- map the process
- split work into skills (LLM) and automations (deterministic)
- define data handoffs (JSON envelope, working CSVs)
- orchestrate the steps with predictable control flow
- make decisions visible (audit trail every step)
- **preserve human review at the right pause points** (specialist
  draft, FAQ promotion)
- **close the institutional-learning loop** (accepted fix → FAQ candidate
  → reviewed FAQ entry)
- expose skills via **multiple front doors** (web demo, MCP) without
  duplicating logic
- test realistic scenarios end-to-end

::: notes
End on the management lesson: AI workflow design is process architecture plus
governance, not only model selection.
:::
